title: Does the EU Pay Transparency Directive require training for managers and HR?
description: What Directive (EU) 2023/970 says about training: recital 30, Article 11 support, the recital 51 remedy, and what HR and hiring managers need to know.
shortAnswer: Directive (EU) 2023/970, the EU Pay Transparency Directive, contains no article requiring employers to train managers or HR staff. Recital 30 asks Member States to make training and tools available to employers, Article 11 obliges Member States to give training to employers with fewer than 250 workers, and recital 51 lists mandatory HR training as a possible court-ordered remedy. Transposition was due by June 7, 2026.
keyTakeaways: There is no employer training duty in the Directive's articles. Training appears in recital 30, recital 51, and Article 11, each directed at Member States or courts rather than at employers.
Article 11 requires Member States to provide technical assistance and training to employers with fewer than 250 workers and to their workers' representatives.

The obligations employers must operate are concrete: no pay history questions (Article 5(2)), pay criteria made accessible (Article 6), information requests answered within two months (Article 7(4)), and gender pay gap reporting from June 7, 2027 for employers with 150 or more workers (Article 9).
Where an employer has not implemented the transparency obligations, Article 18(2) shifts the burden of proof onto the employer in pay discrimination proceedings, which makes manager error costly.
As at November 2026, the EUR-Lex national transposition database listed no notified Portuguese measures for the Directive, with a notice that the collection was being updated.
regulator: European Union legislation, enforced through national law by Member State equality bodies, labor inspectorates and courts
appliesTo: Employers in the public and private sectors in every EU Member State, once national transposing law applies
Workers with an employment contract or relationship, including part-time, fixed-term and temporary agency workers, and managers (recital 18 and Article 2)
Applicants for employment, who gain pre-employment pay information rights (Article 5)
Employers with 100 or more workers, which must report gender pay gap data on a staged timetable (Article 9)

sections.heading: Is there an article that makes employers train managers or HR?

blocks.text: No. None of the 37 articles of [Directive (EU) 2023/970](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32023L0970) obliges an employer to deliver training. The word "training" appears in the operative text only in Article 11, which places a duty on Member States, not employers. Everything else about training sits in the non-binding recitals.

That distinction matters for a training plan. A Member State may go further when it transposes the Directive and add a training requirement in national law, so the national act is the document that settles whether training is mandatory in a given country. At EU level, training is a practical necessity rather than a legal duty: the people who write job adverts, answer pay questions, and set pay need to apply rules that carry a reversed burden of proof if they get them wrong.

blocks.title: Where training is mentioned
blocks.text: Recital 30 (Member States should make training and tools available to employers on work of equal value), recital 51 (mandatory training for HR staff as an example of a remedy), and Article 11 (Member States must provide technical assistance and training to employers with fewer than 250 workers). No recital or article sets content, hours, or frequency for employer-run training.

sections.heading: What do recital 30 and recital 51 actually say?

blocks.text: Recital 30 is about support for employers, and recital 51 is about remedies. Recital 30 reads: "Member States should ensure that training and specific tools and methodologies are made available to support and guide employers in the assessment of what constitutes work of equal value." It adds that this should help "especially for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises" and that Member States may entrust the development of tools to the social partners.

Recital 51 describes structural or organizational measures that a competent authority or national court might require after an infringement. Its examples include reviewing the pay setting mechanism, an action plan to remove gaps, raising workers' awareness of their right to equal pay, and "to establish a mandatory training for human resources staff on equal pay and gender-neutral job evaluation and classification". The operative hook is Article 17(1)(b), which allows an order "to take measures to ensure that the rights or obligations related to the principle of equal pay are applied".

Read together, the recitals point to the topic EU legislators expect HR staff to understand: gender-neutral job evaluation and classification. An employer that trains HR on that topic before any dispute is doing voluntarily what a court could later order.

sections.heading: What does Article 11 require Member States to provide?

blocks.text: Article 11 requires Member States to "provide support, in the form of technical assistance and training, to employers with fewer than 250 workers and to the workers' representatives concerned". It is a duty on governments, and smaller employers can expect national equality bodies or labor ministries to publish guidance, tools, and courses.

Article 4(2) adds a related duty: Member States must, in consultation with equality bodies, ensure that "analytical tools or methodologies are made available and are easily accessible" for assessing and comparing the value of work. Article 4(4) sets the criteria those tools must use: skills, effort, responsibility and working conditions, applied in a gender-neutral way, and "relevant soft skills shall not be undervalued". These criteria are the core content of any internal job evaluation training.

Article 4(3) lets the Commission update Union-wide guidelines on gender-neutral job evaluation in consultation with the European Institute for Gender Equality (EIGE). According to the [European Commission's equal pay page](https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/gender-equality/equal-pay/eu-action-equal-pay_en), the Commission and EIGE launched EU-wide guidelines on gender-neutral job evaluation and classification, tailored to different sizes of employer, on March 26, 2026. The same page says that after the June 7, 2026 deadline the Commission will pay particular attention to the conformity of national legislation. Those guidelines are a sensible starting point for reward team training.

sections.heading: Which employer obligations should training cover, and who needs it?

blocks.text: Training should follow the obligations that individual employees actually perform. The table below maps each operative article to the role that carries it day to day and the evidence an auditor or labor inspector would reasonably expect. It is an original mapping, not an EU template, and national law may add to it.

blocks.text: The roles in the left column map naturally onto a [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix). Hiring managers need the Article 5 rules in their onboarding, line managers need to explain Article 6 criteria and route Article 7 requests, and the reward team needs a deeper module on gender-neutral job evaluation under Article 4.

sections.heading: What are the key dates and thresholds?

blocks.text: The Directive was adopted on May 10, 2023 and published in the Official Journal on May 17, 2023. Under Article 34(1), Member States had to bring national measures into force by June 7, 2026. Reporting duties then phase in by employer size.

blocks.text: Article 7(4) gives employers two months to answer a worker's request for pay information. Article 16(4) states that compensation "shall not be restricted by the fixing of a prior upper limit". Article 18(2) moves the burden of proof to the employer where it has not implemented the obligations in Articles 5, 6, 7, 9 and 10, unless the failure was "manifestly unintentional and of a minor character".

sections.heading: Has Portugal transposed the Pay Transparency Directive?

blocks.text: We could not confirm a Portuguese transposing act as at November 2026. The [EUR-Lex national transposition measures page](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/NIM/?uri=CELEX:32023L0970) for the Directive listed zero notified measures for Portugal when checked, alongside a notice that the collection was being updated and search results might be unreliable. Several other Member States, including Belgium, showed notified measures.

Employers in Portugal should therefore treat the Directive's dates as the reference point, monitor the Diário da República for the transposing law, and check whether it adds training duties. Existing Portuguese equality obligations, covered on the page about [Portugal's equality plans and training](/regulations/portugal-equality-plans-and-training), remain in force in the meantime. A guide on [updating training when regulations change](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change) sets out how to handle a transposing law that arrives late.

sections.heading: How should an employer build pay transparency training without a legal mandate?

blocks.text: Base the program on the obligations that create risk, not on a generic equal pay course. A practical sequence:

items: Confirm the national transposing law in each country of operation and note any training duty it adds.
Identify every role that writes adverts, interviews, sets pay, answers pay questions, or signs off reports.
Teach recruiters and hiring managers the Article 5 rules with real scenarios, including how to respond when a candidate volunteers their salary.
Train the reward team on gender-neutral job evaluation using the Article 4(4) criteria and any national tool published under Article 4(2).
Give line managers a short module on explaining pay criteria and routing information requests within the Article 7(4) deadline.
Keep records that show who was trained on which version, since Article 18(2) makes the employer prove compliance.

blocks.text: Mapping each article to a role and a learning outcome is the method in [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations). The broader EU picture is on the page about [mandatory workplace training in the European Union](/guides/mandatory-workplace-training-in-the-european-union).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each Directive article and its national transposing provision as separate obligations linked to the roles that perform them. When a Member State publishes its law, the affected learning outcomes and learners can be traced from the new provision rather than rebuilt from scratch.

faqs.q: Do line managers need pay transparency training under the Directive?
faqs.a: The Directive does not say so. It places duties on the employer, such as making pay criteria accessible under Article 6 and answering requests within two months under Article 7(4). Line managers often perform those tasks in practice, so most employers will brief them, but the legal duty to train, if any, will come from national transposing law.

faqs.q: Can a court order an employer to train its HR team?
faqs.a: Article 17(1)(b) lets competent authorities or national courts order measures to ensure the equal pay rights and obligations are applied. Recital 51 gives mandatory training for HR staff on equal pay and gender-neutral job evaluation as an example of such a measure. Whether a particular court can make that order depends on national law.

faqs.q: Does the Directive apply to employers with fewer than 100 workers?
faqs.a: Yes, apart from pay gap reporting. The pre-employment, pay criteria and information rights in Articles 5 to 7 apply regardless of size, although Article 6(2) lets Member States exempt employers with fewer than 50 workers from the pay progression part. Article 9(5) allows smaller employers to report voluntarily and lets Member States require it.

faqs.q: Is pay transparency training the same as equal pay training?
faqs.a: It overlaps but is narrower and more procedural. Equal pay training covers the principle in Article 157 TFEU and Directive 2006/54/EC. Pay transparency training adds the Directive's specific procedures: pay ranges for applicants, the ban on pay history questions, annual notices, two month response times, and reporting methodology.
